Roughly speaking, the concrete disadvantages of Olm and Megolm are:

* In the current Matrix implementation, server tells the clients what the group membership is, so a server could spoof an invite to add a malicious user to a room and you'd have to rely on social mechanisms to spot it.

* There's no way to force everyone to rotate the sender key at the same time.

* On the plus side, it decentralises relatively well.

The concrete disadvantages of MLS are:

* Vanilla MLS needs a centralised sequencing function for changing group membership.

* The key bundles are much larger.

* On the plus side, only clients within the group can add new users/devices, and everyone in a given epoch shares the same group secret, so when someone rotates everyone has to rotate to participate in the new epoch.

Now, the server-controlled membership problem can be solved with Olm/Megolm if you instead have the client control the membership, using Matrix itself to define which users are authorised to be in the room, by running the Matrix DAG merge resolution on the client as well as the server. I did this a few weeks ago (in prep for The Matrix Conference next week) to show viability; it works, and has the advantage that you don't have to blow up the whole crypto implementation.

On the other hand, MLS can also be made to decentralise. DiMLS (draft-xue-mls-decentralized) isn't the only option here; DeMLS is the one we've been working with (using the Phoenix DeMLS OpenMLS fork) on the Matrix side - and works by letting MLS epochs fork and then merge again later, using puncturable functions to avoid undermining forward secrecy. This is a much bigger change; we experimented with it a few months back; details here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jc7yfec3iIQ. It's promising, it works, but is much more complex and experimental.

So, TL;DR: it's possible to use olm/megolm securely (even if it's had a mixed record); I doubt strafe is doing fancy client-controlled group membership though. Separately, MLS can be used too, but it is way more complex and has its own complications. On the Matrix side we're still pursuing both (and finally making some progress, although it's a very slow burn).

title: Show HN: BScaff – A CLI tool for project scaffolding and snippets
text:
I built BScaff, a CLI tool for saving and reusing project structures, templates, files, and text snippets. It can serve as a URL bookmark tool as well.

It started with project scaffolding, but I wanted something more general-purpose: a tool that could save almost any reusable starting point and bring it back whenever needed. For each language, I had a specific way of structuring projects that I have refined over years, but I could not find any tool which can quickly help to generate such scaffolding quickly. Copier and Cookiecutter exists but they depend on templates, and I didn't want to create templates for such tasks. One more use-case I had was when I used AI chatbots who suggest some project structure, and I want to quickly create that. So I wanted something offline which can quickly help me save and recreate file trees. Then I added snippets to it too, but I mostly use it for notes taking personally.

Some things you can do with it:

* Save Git repository templates locally and use them offline whenever you need to create a new project

* Create reusable templates from existing directories

* Save and recreate directory structures by copying ASCII file trees and the tool will read it from clipboard and recreate it (or save it for later)

* Save collections of files and generate them again in another directory

* Save text snippets and either copy them to the clipboard or generate files from them

The idea is to avoid repeatedly recreating the same boilerplate, directory structures, configuration files, etc. And you can use it as a note-taking app as well with snippets. It has templates support as well with Jinja-based variable replacement. Template updates are supported, but project updates are not yet implemented, have planned it for future.

It is written in TypeScript, runs on Node.js, and is available on npm.

GitHub: https://github.com/akashnag/bscaff

Install: npm install -g @akashnag/bscaff

Feedback, feature suggestions ( I already have a big backlog though :P ), and contributions are welcome!

Hi HN, I built Merlin to let you use your own Claude Code and Codex subscription from Slack, Linear, and GitHub.

There is a desktop app for macOS and Windows, and a CLI daemon for Linux. When someone mentions Merlin in a Slack thread or Linear issue comment, the task runs on that team member's machine, using their own Claude Code or Codex runtime, and progress and results come back to the original thread. Teammates can steer the agent mid-run. Merlin also has schedules, shared skills, and memory.

I know you've probably heard about Claude Tag. Merlin is similar to that but also different. The model usage goes to the Claude Code or Codex subscription instead of API bill, and you can use Merlin across different surfaces to streamline workflow instead of just in Slack (Linear's agent session works particularly well with Merlin. You can just leverage Linear as your control panel for agentic work using Merlin). Merlin also runs on your local machines, which means that you can use your local context including MCPs, skills and local files instead of in a cloud sandbox.

Merlin does not upload your working directory, and provider credentials stay on the device. The request and the context it needs pass through Merlin. Runtimes start private, and an owner can make one public so teammates, including non-engineers, can use it.

But there're also some limits, and we'll probably deal with them in future updates: - An offline or sleeping machine can't take work. The same issue as OpenClaw. But if you have a mac mini or ec2 setup it should be fine. - Linux is CLI only. We may later add desktop for Linux. - While runtime delegation isn't a problem for now, we're still working on how to make the best use of each team member's local runtime and let them work together cohesively.

We've been internally using Merlin for quite some time. It really helps when you're trying to add some AI juice to the conversation or just delegate things to your agents. I think it reduces the friction of having to do the copying & pasting and switch to another app to ask for AI's input when you're having a discussion in a collaborative environment like Slack or Linear. It's really the fastest way from intent to execution.

Pricing: free for up to 5 active users and 1,000 requests/month. We think this should get small teams started and get real value from it. Team is $59/mo and Scale is $99/mo, with a 14-day Team trial and no credit card required.

Author here. I’ve been running this experiment for a couple of years whenever a new model comes out, and this is the first time the results have been good enough to share.

I provide an LLM with a natural language specification (e.g., "an HTTP server on port 8125"), and a bash loop executes what the model generates; the actual error encountered is then fed back to the model until the test passes. There are three levels: C with gcc, assembly with as + ld, and raw bytes (where the model writes the ELF file directly, with nothing between it and the binary other than `xxd -r`).

The raw bytes level isn't always reliable: in 5 runs using Claude Sonnet 5.5 on x86-64, "Hello, World" succeeded in 4 out of 5 attempts, and the HTTP server in 2 out of 5. The C and assembly levels succeeded in all 5 attempts. The system also executes binaries generated by the model, so please check what the code does before running it.
